questions.stem: On a velocity-time graph, what does a flat horizontal section of the line show?

options.text: Zero acceleration, so the velocity holds a steady value
options.explanation: No tilt means no change of velocity per second: cruising at one constant velocity.

options.text: The object has stopped moving altogether
options.explanation: Stopped would mean the velocity line sits ON the time axis at zero, not merely flat above it.

options.text: The acceleration is at its largest
options.explanation: Largest acceleration belongs to the steepest slope; a flat line has no slope at all.

options.text: The object is decelerating gently
options.explanation: Deceleration needs a downward tilt; a level line has none.

questions.stem: Two straight sections appear on a velocity-time graph: one shallow, one steep, both rising. What do they share and how do they differ?

options.text: Both show constant acceleration; the steeper one has the larger acceleration
options.explanation: Any straight section is constant acceleration, and steepness ranks the acceleration's size.

options.text: Both show the same acceleration because both rise
options.explanation: Rising fixes the sign, not the size; steepness sets how large the acceleration is.

options.text: The shallow one shows deceleration because it changes slowly
options.explanation: A gentle rise is a small positive acceleration, not a negative one.

options.text: Neither shows constant acceleration unless the line is flat
options.explanation: Constancy of acceleration is exactly what a straight section means.

questions.stem: A line on a velocity-time graph tilts steadily downward. What is happening to the object?

options.text: Its velocity is decreasing, so it is decelerating
options.explanation: A negative gradient reads directly as decreasing velocity.

options.text: It is moving backwards along its path
options.explanation: Backwards travel would need the velocity itself to go negative, which a downward tilt alone does not show.

options.text: It is accelerating, because all motion counts as acceleration
options.explanation: Losing speed is deceleration; the sign of the gradient settles which.

options.text: Its velocity is unchanged; only its distance changes
options.explanation: On this graph the vertical axis IS the velocity, so a tilt is a velocity change.

questions.stem: Which quantity belongs on the vertical axis of a velocity-time graph?

options.text: Velocity, in metres per second
options.explanation: The graph is named for its axes: velocity up, time along.

options.text: Distance travelled, in metres
options.explanation: Distance on the vertical axis makes it a distance-time graph, the sibling graph from earlier in this section.

options.text: Acceleration, in m/s²
options.explanation: Acceleration is read FROM the gradient here; it is not the plotted quantity.

options.text: Time, in seconds
options.explanation: Time always runs along the horizontal axis on these motion graphs.

questions.stem: A graph shows a straight rising section followed by a flat section. How should the two sections be described?

options.text: Constant acceleration first, then constant velocity
options.explanation: The rising straight is steady acceleration; the flat continuation is steady velocity.

options.text: Increasing acceleration first, then acceleration
options.explanation: A straight rise has one fixed acceleration; only a curve steepens.

options.text: Constant velocity first, then deceleration
options.explanation: That reverses both sections; the flat stretch comes second in this graph.

options.text: Deceleration first, then rest
options.explanation: A rising tilt and a flat line above the axis are neither deceleration nor rest.

questions.stem: State what a straight sloping line on a velocity-time graph tells you about the acceleration.
questions.modelAnswer: A straight sloping line means the acceleration is constant: the velocity changes by the same amount every second along that section.

questions.stem: Recall what the steepness of the slope on a velocity-time graph represents.
questions.modelAnswer: The steepness (slope) represents the magnitude of the acceleration: a steep slope is a large acceleration and a gentle slope is a small one.

questions.stem: Explain why a flat line and a line sitting on the time axis describe two different physical situations on a velocity-time graph.
questions.modelAnswer: A flat line above the axis fixes the velocity at some non-zero steady value: the object cruises. A line lying on the time axis fixes the velocity at zero: the object is at rest. The height of the flat stretch is the velocity itself, so height, not flatness, separates cruising from stopping.

questions.stem: A velocity-time graph shows an object held at 15 m/s for 8 s, then rising in a straight line to 25 m/s over the next 10 s. Describe both sections and state which section has the larger acceleration.
questions.modelAnswer: The first section is constant velocity (zero acceleration) at 15 m/s for 8 s; the second is a straight rise, a constant acceleration of (25 − 15) / 10 = 1.0 m/s². The second section has the larger acceleration, since the first has none.

questions.stem: Which reading must be taken from the vertical axis when extracting acceleration from a velocity-time gradient?

options.text: The change in velocity across the chosen section
options.explanation: Δy is the velocity change; it is the numerator of the gradient and of a = Δv/t.

options.text: The velocity at the start of the whole graph
options.explanation: The starting velocity of the graph is irrelevant; only the change across the section enters.

options.text: The highest velocity anywhere on the plot
options.explanation: A peak value is not the section's change; the triangle fixes which two heights matter.

options.text: The area beneath the line
options.explanation: Area belongs to the distance reading of the next lesson, not to the gradient.

questions.stem: A straight section carries the velocity from 8 m/s up to 20 m/s across 6 s. What acceleration does the gradient give?

options.explanation: Δv = 12 m/s over Δt = 6 s gives a gradient of 2.0 m/s².

options.text: 3.3 m/s², from 20 ÷ 6
options.explanation: Dividing the final velocity by the time ignores the 8 m/s the object already had.

options.text: 0.50 m/s², from 6 ÷ 12
options.explanation: That inverts the quotient; the velocity change divides by the time.

options.text: 12 m/s², quoting the velocity change as the rate
options.explanation: 12 m/s is Δv; the division by 6 s is what makes it a rate.

questions.stem: Why do examiners prefer a large gradient triangle drawn on the graph?

options.text: A larger triangle spreads the readings across more gridlines, so each read value is more reliable
options.explanation: Bigger rises and runs mean the same half-square-line reading error is a smaller fraction of each value.

options.text: Large triangles make the gradient come out positive
options.explanation: The sign comes from the tilt, not the triangle's size.

options.text: Small triangles are banned by the mark scheme
options.explanation: Nothing is banned; small triangles just lose precision and credit for the drawn construction.

options.text: A large triangle removes the need to state units
options.explanation: Units are always required on the final acceleration, whatever the triangle's size.

questions.stem: On the cyclist's training graph, the section between 5 s and 10 s rises by 5 m/s. What acceleration does that section carry?

options.text: 1 m/s², from 5 m/s over 5 s
options.explanation: Δv = 5 m/s and Δt = 10 − 5 = 5 s, so a = 5/5 = 1 m/s².

options.text: 5 m/s², from 5 ÷ 1
options.explanation: The 5 in the denominator must be the 5-second interval, not a bare 1.

options.text: 0.5 m/s², from 5 ÷ 10
options.explanation: Dividing by the absolute timestamp 10 s forgets that the section starts at 5 s.

options.text: 2 m/s², from 10 ÷ 5
options.explanation: That divides the timestamps rather than the changes; the quotient must be Δv over Δt.

questions.stem: A gradient triangle is drawn on a downward-sloping section. The velocity falls 6 m/s across 3 s. What should be concluded?

options.text: The gradient is −2 m/s²: a deceleration of 2 m/s²
options.explanation: The fall of 6 m/s across 3 s gives a signed gradient of −2 m/s², read as decelerating at 2 m/s².

options.text: The gradient is +2 m/s² because the triangle is drawn upward
options.explanation: The construction is drawn for measurement; the sign comes from the falling velocity.

options.text: The gradient is −18 m/s², multiplying 6 by 3
options.explanation: Gradient divides the changes; multiplication has no place in the reading.

options.text: No acceleration can be found from a falling line
options.explanation: Falling lines carry perfectly good negative gradients; the method is unchanged.

questions.stem: State the relationship between a velocity-time gradient and acceleration in symbols.
questions.modelAnswer: Acceleration = gradient = Δy / Δx, where Δy is the change in velocity and Δx is the change in time across the straight section.

questions.stem: Recall the two practical instructions for drawing a gradient triangle on an exam graph.
questions.modelAnswer: Draw it as large as the section allows, and take both the velocity change and the time change directly from the axis scales with their units.

questions.stem: Explain why one single gradient value can describe a whole straight section of a velocity-time graph.
questions.modelAnswer: Along a straight line the gradient is the same at every point, and on this graph that gradient IS the acceleration. A straight section therefore has one unchanging acceleration, so one triangle anywhere on the section returns the value that holds for the entire interval.

questions.stem: A tram's velocity falls from 18 m/s to 6 m/s in a straight section lasting 4.0 s. Use the gradient to calculate the acceleration and state the motion word for it.
questions.modelAnswer: Δv = 6 − 18 = −12 m/s over Δt = 4.0 s, so the gradient is −3.0 m/s²; the negative value is a deceleration.
